plain: A flat curved bone running from the spine around to the front. Ribs 3 to 9 all share the same pattern, so learn one and you know them all.
detail: A typical rib has a head with two facets (articulating with its own vertebra and the one above), a neck, a tubercle that articulates with the transverse process, a sharply curved angle, and a shaft. Its lower border carries the costal groove.
clinical: The costal groove holds the intercostal vein, artery and nerve, in that order from above downwards — VAN. That is why a chest drain or needle is inserted immediately ABOVE a rib, along its upper border, to avoid the neurovascular bundle tucked under the rib above.

plain: The rib that meets the breastbone exactly at the ridge you can feel where the top of the sternum joins its body.
detail: Thinner and about twice as long as the first rib. Its outer surface carries a roughened tuberosity for the first digitation of serratus anterior.
clinical: Its cartilage attaches at the sternal angle, so finding that ridge and sliding sideways is how you identify the 2nd rib — and from there count every other rib and intercostal space.

plain: A rib that does not reach the breastbone on its own. Its cartilage joins onto the cartilage of the rib above instead.
detail: Ribs 8, 9 and 10 are the false (vertebrochondral) ribs. Their costal cartilages join the cartilage above rather than the sternum directly, forming the costal margin. The 10th usually has a single facet on its head.
clinical: Ribs 1–7 are true (vertebrosternal), 8–10 false (vertebrochondral), 11–12 floating (free). The costal margin formed by ribs 7–10 is the surface landmark for the lower border of the thorax.

plain: The two short bottom ribs that end freely in the muscle of the abdominal wall, with no attachment at the front at all.
detail: Short, with a single facet on the head, and no neck, tubercle or angle. They end in pointed tips capped by cartilage, lying free in the posterior abdominal wall.
clinical: The 12th rib is the surgeon's landmark for the posterior approach to the kidney. It also means the pleura can be entered during a loin incision if the rib is mistaken for the 11th.

plain: Bars of springy cartilage joining the front ends of the ribs to the breastbone. They are what let the chest expand when you breathe in.
detail: Hyaline cartilage. The first seven reach the sternum directly; the 8th, 9th and 10th attach to the cartilage above, forming the costal margin.
clinical: They calcify and ossify with age, stiffening the chest wall and reducing the elasticity of breathing in older people. Their calcification on a chest X-ray is a rough guide to age.

plain: The broad upper part of the breastbone. The dip you can feel at the base of your throat is its top edge.
detail: Carries the jugular (suprasternal) notch, the clavicular notches for the sternoclavicular joints, and a facet for the 1st costal cartilage. It joins the body of the sternum at the manubriosternal joint.
clinical: The ridge at that joint is the sternal angle (angle of Louis) — arguably the single most useful landmark in the thorax. It lies at the level of the 2nd costal cartilage and the T4/T5 disc, marking the aortic arch, the bifurcation of the trachea, and the start and end of the arch.

plain: The long flat middle part of the breastbone, sitting just under the skin at the front of the chest.
detail: Runs from the sternal angle above to the xiphisternal joint below, receiving the 2nd to 7th costal cartilages at its edges.
clinical: Because it is subcutaneous and overlies red marrow, it is a site for sternal marrow biopsy. It is also where the heel of the hand is placed for chest compressions, over its lower half.

plain: The top neck bone, shaped like a ring. It carries the skull, and it is the joint that lets you nod yes.
detail: A ring with no body and no spinous process — anterior and posterior arches joined by two lateral masses. Its superior facets receive the occipital condyles at the atlanto-occipital joint.
clinical: Nodding ('yes') happens at the atlanto-occipital joint. A burst fracture of the ring from an axial blow to the head is a Jefferson fracture.

plain: The second neck bone. It has a peg pointing upwards that the atlas spins around — this is the joint that lets you shake your head no.
detail: Its dens (odontoid process) projects up into the ring of the atlas, held against the anterior arch by the transverse ligament of the atlas.
clinical: Rotation ('no') happens at the atlanto-axial joint. A fractured dens, or rupture of the transverse ligament in rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome, allows the dens to compress the spinal cord — which is why the neck is handled so carefully in those patients.

plain: The small neck vertebrae. Each has a hole in its side process that no other vertebra has — the artery to the brain runs up through them.
detail: Identified by the foramen transversarium in each transverse process, a triangular vertebral foramen, and bifid spinous processes from C3 to C6. C7 is the vertebra prominens, with a long single spine you can feel at the base of the neck.
clinical: The vertebral artery ascends through the foramina transversaria of C6 up to C1, then enters the skull. C7's prominent spine is the standard surface landmark for counting vertebral levels.

plain: The twelve chest vertebrae. They are the only ones with ribs attached, and they have long spines that slope steeply downwards like roof tiles.
detail: Recognised by costal facets on the sides of the bodies (for rib heads) and on the transverse processes (for rib tubercles), a circular vertebral foramen, and long downward-sloping spinous processes.
clinical: Their spines overlap so steeply that the tip of a mid-thoracic spine lies at the level of the vertebral body below — which matters when localising a level from the surface.

plain: The five big lower back vertebrae. They carry the most weight, so their bodies are the largest of all.
detail: Massive kidney-shaped bodies, no costal facets and no foramen transversarium, short blunt spines, and sagittally oriented facet joints that permit flexion and extension but very little rotation.
clinical: The highest points of the iliac crests lie at the L4 level. That line guides lumbar puncture at L3/L4 or L4/L5 — safely below the conus medullaris, which ends at about L1/L2 in adults.

plain: A large triangular bone made of five vertebrae fused into one. It wedges between the two hip bones and transmits your body weight to the legs.
detail: Five fused sacral vertebrae. Its auricular surfaces meet the hip bones at the sacro-iliac joints. The sacral canal ends below at the sacral hiatus, and the prominent front edge of S1 is the sacral promontory.
clinical: The sacral hiatus is the entry point for caudal epidural anaesthesia. The sacral promontory is the landmark used to measure the pelvic inlet in obstetrics.

plain: The small tailbone at the very bottom of the spine, usually four tiny vertebrae fused together.
detail: Three to five rudimentary vertebrae, commonly four. Gives attachment to the coccygeus and levator ani muscles and the anococcygeal ligament.
clinical: Bruised or fractured by falling onto the buttocks, and often injured during childbirth. The resulting coccydynia can be persistent.

plain: The bone of the forehead. It also forms the roofs of both eye sockets and contains an air sinus above each eyebrow.
detail: Forms the forehead, the roofs of the orbits and the anterior cranial fossa floor. Meets the parietal bones at the coronal suture. Contains the frontal sinuses.
clinical: Frontal sinusitis causes pain and tenderness over the eyebrow, worse on bending forwards. In infants the two halves are separated by the metopic suture, which usually closes by about six years.

plain: The two large curved bones forming most of the roof and sides of the skull.
detail: Meet each other at the sagittal suture, the frontal bone at the coronal suture, and the occipital bone at the lambdoid suture.
clinical: Where the parietal, frontal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet is the pterion — the thinnest part of the skull, with the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery running just underneath. A blow there can rupture it and cause an extradural haematoma.

plain: The bone at the side of the skull around the ear. It houses the whole of the hearing and balance apparatus inside its densest part.
detail: Has squamous, petrous, mastoid, tympanic and styloid parts. Contains the middle and inner ear, the external acoustic meatus, and the mandibular fossa for the temporomandibular joint.
clinical: The facial nerve runs through the facial canal within it, so a petrous temporal fracture can cause facial palsy along with deafness and CSF otorrhoea. Mastoid air cells communicate with the middle ear, allowing infection to spread to mastoiditis.

plain: The bone at the back and base of the skull. It has the big hole through which the brainstem becomes the spinal cord.
detail: Contains the foramen magnum, flanked by the occipital condyles that articulate with the atlas. Carries the external occipital protuberance and the nuchal lines for neck muscle attachment.
clinical: Raised intracranial pressure can force the cerebellar tonsils down through the foramen magnum — coning — compressing the medulla and its respiratory centres. This is why lumbar puncture is avoided when pressure is raised.

plain: A butterfly-shaped bone wedged across the middle of the skull base. It holds the pituitary gland in a saddle on its upper surface.
detail: Body, greater and lesser wings, and pterygoid processes. Its sella turcica houses the pituitary. Transmits the optic canal, superior orbital fissure, and foramina rotundum, ovale and spinosum.
clinical: It articulates with almost every other skull bone, which is why it is called the keystone of the cranium. A pituitary tumour expanding out of the sella compresses the optic chiasma above it, classically causing bitemporal hemianopia.

plain: A light, spongy bone between the eyes. Its top plate is perforated like a sieve to let the smell nerves through.
detail: Cribriform plate, perpendicular plate, ethmoidal labyrinth with air cells, and the superior and middle nasal conchae. The crista galli projects upwards for the falx cerebri.
clinical: Olfactory nerve filaments pass through the cribriform plate, so a fracture there shears them and causes anosmia, often with CSF rhinorrhoea. The perpendicular plate forms the upper part of the nasal septum.

plain: A thin plough-shaped bone forming the lower back part of the wall between the two nostrils.
detail: Forms the posteroinferior part of the bony nasal septum, with the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above it and the septal cartilage in front.
clinical: Deviation of the septum most often involves the junction between the vomer, the ethmoid plate and the septal cartilage.

plain: The lower jaw — the only bone of the skull that moves.
detail: Body and two rami. The head of each ramus forms the temporomandibular joint. The mandibular foramen on the inner ramus admits the inferior alveolar nerve, which emerges at the mental foramen.
clinical: An inferior alveolar nerve block is injected at the mandibular foramen for lower-teeth dentistry. The mandible commonly fractures in two places at once because it is a ring of bone — always look for a second fracture.

plain: The upper jaw. The two maxillae together carry the upper teeth, form most of the hard palate, and make the floor of both eye sockets.
detail: Body with frontal, zygomatic, alveolar and palatine processes. Contains the maxillary sinus, the largest paranasal sinus, and transmits the infraorbital nerve through the infraorbital foramen.
clinical: The maxillary sinus drains through an opening high on its medial wall, so it drains poorly when upright and is the sinus most often infected. Because its floor is close to the upper molar roots, dental infection can spread into it.

plain: The cheekbone. It forms the prominence of the cheek and the outer wall and floor of the eye socket.
detail: Articulates with the frontal, maxillary, temporal and sphenoid bones. Its temporal process joins the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch.
clinical: A blow to the cheek produces a tripod fracture, separating it at all three of its main attachments. Flattening of the cheek and a step in the orbital rim are the signs.

plain: One of the two small bones forming the bridge of the nose. Everything below them is cartilage.
detail: Small oblong bones meeting in the midline, articulating with the frontal bone above and the maxillae at the sides.
clinical: The most commonly fractured bone of the face.

plain: The smallest bone of the face, a fingernail-sized plate in the inner wall of the eye socket where tears drain away.
detail: Forms part of the medial wall of the orbit. With the maxilla it makes the fossa for the lacrimal sac, leading into the nasolacrimal canal.
clinical: The nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior meatus of the nose — which is why your nose runs when you cry.

plain: The collarbone. It is the only bony strut joining the arm to the rest of the skeleton, holding the shoulder out away from the chest.
detail: An S-shaped bone, convex forwards medially and concave forwards laterally. Articulates with the manubrium medially and the acromion laterally.
clinical: The first bone in the body to begin ossifying and the last to complete it, at around 25. It usually fractures at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds, the weakest point: the medial fragment is pulled up by sternocleidomastoid and the lateral fragment drops under the weight of the limb.

plain: The shoulder blade — a flat triangular bone that glides over the back of the ribs rather than being locked to them.
detail: Carries the spine, which ends laterally as the acromion, the hook-like coracoid process in front, and the shallow glenoid cavity for the head of the humerus.
clinical: Its mobility depends on serratus anterior holding it against the chest wall. If the long thoracic nerve is injured, the medial border lifts away — winging of the scapula.

plain: The single bone of the upper arm. Several major nerves lie directly against it, so its fractures are known by which nerve they injure.
detail: Head, anatomical and surgical necks, greater and lesser tubercles, radial (spiral) groove, and the medial and lateral epicondyles at the elbow.
clinical: Three nerves, three levels: surgical neck fracture injures the axillary nerve; mid-shaft fracture injures the radial nerve in the spiral groove, causing wrist drop; medial epicondyle fracture injures the ulnar nerve. A supracondylar fracture in a child endangers the brachial artery and median nerve.

plain: The large flared bone of the pelvis. It starts as three separate bones that fuse together in the socket for the hip joint.
detail: Ilium, ischium and pubis, fusing at the acetabulum through the triradiate cartilage, which closes at about 15 to 16 years. Carries the iliac crest, anterior superior iliac spine, ischial tuberosity and pubic symphysis.
clinical: The iliac crest is a standard site for bone marrow aspiration and for harvesting bone graft. The ischial tuberosity is what you sit on, and the ischial spine is the landmark for a pudendal nerve block in obstetrics.

plain: The thigh bone — the longest, heaviest and strongest bone in the body. Its neck is the weak point, and it breaks easily in old age.
detail: Head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, shaft with the linea aspera behind, and the medial and lateral condyles below. The neck meets the shaft at about 125 degrees.
clinical: The head is supplied mainly by retinacular vessels running up along the neck. A fractured neck tears them, so the head can undergo avascular necrosis — which is why these fractures are often treated by replacing the head rather than fixing it. The limb lies shortened and externally rotated.

plain: The shin bone. It carries essentially all the weight passing down the leg, and its front edge lies directly under the skin.
detail: Medial and lateral condyles above, tibial tuberosity in front for the patellar ligament, a sharp subcutaneous anterior border, and the medial malleolus below.
clinical: Because the anteromedial surface is subcutaneous, tibial fractures are frequently open, and the poor soft-tissue cover makes infection and delayed union common. The medial malleolus is the bony prominence on the inner ankle.

plain: The slender outer bone of the leg. It carries almost no weight — its job is muscle attachment and making the outer wall of the ankle joint.
detail: Head, neck, shaft and the lateral malleolus, which descends further than the medial malleolus and forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise.
clinical: The common fibular nerve winds round its neck against bare bone, so a fracture there or a tight cast causes foot drop. Because it bears so little weight, the fibula is a favoured donor site for bone grafts.

plain: The heel bone, and the largest bone of the foot. It takes the impact every time your heel strikes the ground.
detail: Articulates with the talus above and the cuboid in front. Its posterior surface receives the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, and the sustentaculum tali supports the talus medially.
clinical: Fractured by falling from a height onto the heels. Always examine the spine as well — the same fall commonly produces a compression fracture of a lumbar vertebra.

plain: The bone that links the leg to the foot. Remarkably, not a single muscle attaches to it.
detail: Head, neck and body. Its trochlea sits in the ankle mortise between the two malleoli, and it transmits the entire body weight to the foot. No muscles attach to it, so it is covered in articular cartilage over much of its surface.
clinical: Its blood supply enters distally and runs backwards, like the scaphoid. A fracture through the neck can therefore cut off the body's supply and cause avascular necrosis.
